messages.subject: procD.pgls null model and interpretation of r2
messages.subject_clean: procD.pgls null model and interpretation of r2
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've hit a few snags in my analysis and I'm hoping someone can shed some light on a couple of geomorph-related questions. The first is pretty straightforward: is there a way to run a null model through the procD.pgls function in geomorph? I'm trying to separately phylogenetically correct a multivariate (shape) and a univariate (size) data set. While the gls function in 'nlme' will run on a null model, it cannot accommodate multivariate data sets. I feel uncomfortable comparing data phylogenetically corrected in two separate packages as I'm not sure the implementation is equivalent.

Secondly, it has come to my attention that the interpretation of the r2 value is not equivalent between OLS and GLS -- does geomorph incorporate a correction for this or is the reported r2 value computed as it would be with an OLS? Essentially, is it valid to interpret the coefficient of determination from procD.pgls as a percentage of the total variance of the dependent variable explained by the regression?

Any help is much appreciated!

Thanks,
Sarah

messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] procD.pgls null model and interpretation of r2
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sarah,

>
> I've hit a few snags in my analysis and I'm hoping someone can shed some light on a couple of geomorph-related questions. The first is pretty straightforward: is there a way to run a null model through the procD.pgls function in geomorph?

There really is no way to "run a null model”, as procD.pgls needs at least two models - one a null and another with some independent variable - to compare.  Are you asking for linear model coefficients?  If so, then procD.pgls gives you the tools to do that.

For example, follow the example in procD.pgls up until the part you have created pleth.pgls.

Then, pleth.pgls$Pcor is the matrix for phylogenetic correction; pleth.pgls$Y is the matrix of shape data; pleth.pgls$X is the design matrix.  You can do something like this:

P <- pleth.plgs$Pcor
X.null <- as.matrix(pleth.pgls$X[,1] # just the intercept
Y <- pleth.pgls$Y

lm.fit(P%*%X.null, P%*%Y)

which will give you coefficients, fitted values, etc.

>
> Secondly, it has come to my attention that the interpretation of the r2 value is not equivalent between OLS and GLS -- does geomorph incorporate a correction for this or is the reported r2 value computed as it would be with an OLS? Essentially, is it valid to interpret the coefficient of determination from procD.pgls as a percentage of the total variance of the dependent variable explained by the regression?
>

procD.pgls calculates R-squared values as SSeffect/SStotal, where SS is based on phylogenetically corrected values.  So, no, the values will not be the same as in OLS.  To my way of thinking, it is valid, but I would change your last part of the question to "percentage of the total varianceation of the dependent variable explained by the regression, after adjusting values due to phylogenetic relatedness.”

Hope that helps
Mike

messages.subject: Two different means
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Why are these not the same thing?

mu <- gpagen(X, Proj=FALSE)$consensus
mu2 <- mshape(gpagen(X, Proj=FALSE)$coords)

... but these are

mu <- gpagen(X, Proj=TRUE)$consensus
mu2 <- mshape(gpagen(X, Proj=TRUE)$coords)

It relates to the fact that when tangent projection is turned off (FALSE), the centroid size of the mshape-derived mean is not 1.

Thanks.

David

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Two different means
messages.body_plain:
David,

The reason is that proj=FALSE retains the specimens in shape space which is curved. Thus, the mshape obtained from these will actually be found inside the shape space and not on it. As an analogy, imagine finding the measure of central tendency of points on part of a circle: the arithmetic mean is inside the circle, not on it.  Rohlf 1999 has some conceptual graphics that relate to the projection and scaling in GPA which relates to this.

Now if you notice, the consensus configuration, even from proj=FALSE is identical to all of the proj=TRUE mean estimates. This is because the consensus used during GPA is at unit centroid size, meaning it is a point on shape space. It is also the point of tangency with tangent space, so these 3 all match up.

Basically, the second option of the 4 you list is different from the rest because it is incorrect. The mean of the shapes on the curved shape space is a mean shape, but is not of unit centroid size. Hence the different coordinates.

Hope this helps.

Dean

E.g.,

mu2 <- geomorph:::cs.scale(mshape(gpagen(X, Proj=FALSE)$coords))

This changes mu2 to be unit size, like the consensus.

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Trouble warping mean shape into PC axes
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Trouble warping mean shape into PC axes
messages.body_plain:
Pablo,

This is telling you that your mesh is missing the ‘vb’ components.

Typically, the order of operations is:

1: read in data

2: perform GPA and obtain reference shape

3: read in 3D mesh for some specimen

4: use warpRefMesh() to warp the 3D ply mesh from that specimen to the reference

   Example: warpRefMesh(myply,scallops[,,1], ref, color=NULL,  centered=T)

5: use this mesh in the PCA for graphics.

The geomorph user guide has additional comments on usage: https://github.com/geomorphR/geomorph/wiki

Hope this helps.

Dean

Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Trouble warping mean shape into PC axes

Dear Geomorph team and users

I am trying to use the function WarpRefMesh in order to visualize the shape changes along PC axes. I used the PCA function  pca.x$coords <- plotTangentSpace(proc$coords, label=TRUE,mesh=x), which incorporates the function mesh in this case x which is a .ply mesh of a sectioned hominin molar. However, the analysis shed this error although the PCA plot appear along with RGL device but without the warped mesh.

Warping mesh to negative end of axis 1

Error in t.default(mesh$vb) : el argumento no es una matriz

Can anyone make a suggestion on how to solve this?

thanks in adavance

Pablo

messages.subject_clean: STATS COURSE - Geometric morphometric using R - delivered by Dean Adams, Michael Collyer and Antigoni Kaliontzopoulou
messages.body_plain:
Geometric Morphometrics Using R (GMMR01)

This course is being delivered by Prof. Dean Adams, Prof. Michael Collyer and Dr. Antigoni Kaliontzopoulou

This course will run from 5th - 9th June 2017 at Millport Field centre on the Isle of Cumbre, Scotland. Please note that although the course is held on an island it is extremely accessible and easy to reach using public transport.

The field of geometric morphometrics (GM) is concerned with the quantification and analysis of patterns of shape variation, and its covariation with other variables. Over the past several decades these approaches have become a mainstay in the field of ecology, evolutionary biology, and anthropology, and a panoply of analytical tools for addressing specific biological hypotheses concerning shape have been developed. The goal of this is to provide participants with a working knowledge of the theory of geometric morphometrics, as well as practical training in the application of these methods.

The course is organized in both theoretical and practical sessions. The theoretical sessions will provide a comprehensive introduction to the methods of landmark-based geometric morphometrics, which aims at providing the participants with a solid theoretical background for understanding the procedures used in shape data analysis. Practical sessions will include worked examples, giving the participants the opportunity to gain hands-on experience in the treatment of shape data using the R package geomorph. These sessions focus on the generation of shape variables from primary landmark data, the statistical treatment of shape variation with respect to biological hypotheses, and the visualization of patterns of shape variation and of the shapes themselves for interpretation of statistical findings, using the R language for statistical programming. While practice datasets will be available, it is strongly recommended that participants come with their own datasets.

Note: Because this is a geometric morphometrics workshop in R, it is required that participants have some working knowledge in R. The practical sessions of the course will focus on GM-based analyses, and not basic R user-interfacing. It is therefore strongly recommended that participants refresh their R skills prior to attending the workshop.

Course only and all-inclusive packages (with accommodation and meals) are available.

Course Programme
